## Executive Summary

::: {.hero}
```{=html}
<div class="hero-title">Executive Summary</div>
<div class="framing-callout framing-callout--compact">
<strong>Framing.</strong> Job postings proxy skill <strong>demand</strong>; BUR trainings proxy subsidised skill <strong>supply</strong>. We compare the <strong>mix of skills</strong> on each side after mapping to ESCO (and Lightcast for AI), not absolute volumes.
</div>
```

This report analyses labour demand and supply in Poland through the lens
of online job advertisements and training provision data. It combines
web-scraped vacancy data from <a class="paper-link" href="https://www.pracuj.pl/" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer">Pracuj.pl</a>,
the largest online job portal in Poland, with information from the
<a class="paper-link" href="https://uslugirozwojowe.parp.gov.pl/" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer">Baza Usług Rozwojowych (BUR)</a>,
the country's main database of training and upskilling services. The analysis
focuses on how employers signal required skills and how these relate to
the skills offered through the training system in 2025.

The study integrates labour market analysis with modern NLP methods,
including automated text processing, classification, and LLM-assisted
skill extraction, to transform unstructured job postings and training
descriptions into comparable measures of skill demand and skill supply.

Using mappings to two skill taxonomies, ESCO and Lightcast, the report
compares the composition of requested and supplied skills across
occupations, with particular attention to digital competencies and
emerging skill needs. It also introduces indicators of relative labour
demand, derived from job posting intensity, and contrasts them with the
structure of available training.

The Polish labour market is undergoing rapid transformation, with
increasing digitalization shaping both hiring practices and skill
development pathways. Online job postings provide a timely proxy for
employer demand, while training data from BUR offers insight into the
supply of skills and reskilling opportunities, enabling a joint
assessment of potential mismatches between demand and supply.
:::

## Data Coverage

::: {.section-card}
### Data collection

We collect job advertisements from
<a class="paper-link" href="https://www.pracuj.pl/" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer">Pracuj.pl</a>,
the largest online job portal in Poland, and training-service listings
from
<a class="paper-link" href="https://uslugirozwojowe.parp.gov.pl/" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer">Baza Usług Rozwojowych</a>,
the country's main public database of training and upskilling services.
The analytical sample shown in this report focuses on records that can
be assigned to Polish voivodeships and linked to the regional demand and
supply comparison.

For job advertisements, we retain records with sufficient textual
content to support downstream NLP processing, including job titles and
descriptions. For BUR, we use training-service records with usable
regional metadata and service descriptions. We remove duplicates and
standardize core fields before the records enter the analytical
pipeline.

## Methodology

{{< include includes/wb_slides_methodology.qmd >}}

{{< include includes/wb_methodology_extended.qmd >}}

::: {.section-card}
### Processing pipeline

Raw job postings and training descriptions contain noisy, unstructured
information in Polish (and occasionally English or other languages). We
transform them into a standardised analytic dataset in six steps: we
first identify the source language, translate non-Polish text into
Polish, isolate skill-relevant sentences, map extracted skills to the
ESCO and Lightcast skill taxonomies, standardise job titles to ESCO
occupations using both titles and skill context for disambiguation, and
then enrich each record with sector codes and regional information for
voivodeship-level comparison.

Each step is described in detail below.

:::: {#pipeline-step-01 .step-detail}
#### [Step 01]{.step-badge .step-badge-blue} Language detection

Although the vast majority of postings on Pracuj.pl are in Polish, a
non-trivial share contains English-language titles, mixed-language
descriptions, or occasional postings in other languages. Reliable
identification of the language in which each posting was written ensures
that postings already in Polish can proceed directly to analysis, while
those in other languages are routed to translation.

We apply a machine-learning-based language detector (<a class="paper-link" href="https://github.com/pemistahl/lingua-py" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer">Lingua<span class="source-link-ext">↗</span></a>)
independently to both the job title and the full job description of
every posting. Per-field detection allows us to handle the common case
where a title is in English but the body is in Polish. This is important
because mixed-language postings are common in online vacancies, and
Lingua performs well even when different parts of the same offer use
different languages.
::::

:::: {#pipeline-step-02 .step-detail}
#### [Step 02]{.step-badge .step-badge-amber} Translation

Ensuring that all postings are available in Polish before downstream
processing is essential for consistent skill extraction. While the
majority of Pracuj.pl postings are already in Polish, a subset
(particularly in multinational companies or IT roles) uses English or
mixed-language text. With a corpus of **~750,000 job ads**, machine
translation is a practical necessity for harmonising the linguistic
input to downstream NLP steps. Recent research indicates that LLM-based
translation systems can deliver high-quality machine translation at
scale
(<a class="paper-link" href="https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1007/978-3-031-44693-1_30" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer">Huang et al. (2023)<span class="source-link-ext">↗</span></a>).

Postings already detected as Polish pass through unchanged. All
remaining postings are translated with <a class="paper-link" href="https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/technology/developers-tools/translategemma/" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer">Gemma 3 Translate 4B<span class="source-link-ext">↗</span></a>, an open
source multilingual translation model designed for high-quality
instruction following and strong performance across typologically
different languages. Both **job titles** and **job descriptions** are
translated into Polish and stored alongside the originals to allow
back-referencing when analysts need to inspect the source text. This
ensures that all downstream steps, including skill extraction and title
standardisation, operate on a common-language representation.

To validate translation quality, we conducted a **back-translation**
exercise on a small random sample. In this check,
texts were translated from English into Polish and then back into
English, allowing us to verify that the meaning of skills, occupations,
and task descriptions was preserved with minimal drift.

```{mermaid}
%%| fig-cap: "Translation routing"
%%{init: {'flowchart': {'htmlLabels': true, 'nodeSpacing': 40, 'rankSpacing': 50}} }%%
flowchart LR
    A["Raw posting"] --> B{"Language<br/>detected?"}
    B -->|"Already Polish"| C["Keep original text"]
    B -->|"English / other"| D["Gemma 3 Translate 4B"]
    D -->|"title + description"| E["Translated Polish text"]
    C --> F["Unified Polish corpus"]
    E --> F
```
::::

:::: {#pipeline-step-03 .step-detail}
#### [Step 03]{.step-badge .step-badge-teal} Skill-sentence filtering

Job descriptions typically mix skill requirements with administrative
content such as benefits, company history, or application instructions.
Isolating the skill-relevant sentences before downstream mapping
reduces noise and improves the precision of the extracted skill
profiles.

We use a fine-tuned BERT classifier based on the
<a class="paper-link" href="https://dl.acm.org/doi/abs/10.1145/3672608.3707960" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer">Malandri et al. (2025)<span class="source-link-ext">↗</span></a>
SkillLess approach and the
<a class="paper-link" href="https://huggingface.co/serino28/BERT-OJA-SkillLess" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer">BERT-OJA-SkillLess<span class="source-link-ext">↗</span></a>.
The model performs binary sentence-level classification,
labelling each sentence as either skill-relevant or non-skill.
In our sample, approximately 40--60 % of description text is
filtered out as non-skill content. Only the retained sentences
proceed to the ESCO mapping step.
::::

:::: {#pipeline-step-04 .step-detail}
#### [Step 04]{.step-badge .step-badge-violet} ESCO skill mapping

The European Skills, Competences, Qualifications and Occupations
(<a class="paper-link" href="https://esco.ec.europa.eu/" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer">ESCO<span class="source-link-ext">↗</span></a>) taxonomy provides a standardised
vocabulary of roughly 13,000 skills and competences maintained by the
European Commission. Mapping extracted skill sentences to ESCO entries
creates a common analytical framework that enables direct comparison
across countries and languages.

We employ a **custom contrastive bi-encoder** trained on a massive
synthetic dataset comprising hundreds of thousands of ESCO-labelled
examples derived from the ESCO classification structure. The
bi-encoder learns a **shared representation space** for two different
objects --- job-ad sentences and standardised ESCO skill labels --- by
bringing semantically matching pairs closer together while pushing
non-matching pairs apart. In practical terms, consider a job-ad sentence such as
*"experience with SQL and data visualisation"*. The model learns to
place it close to the correct ESCO entries --- *"use query languages"*
and *"manage databases"* --- and away from everything else. Crucially,
the training signal is strongest for **hard negatives**: skills that
are semantically nearby but not a correct match, such as *"use
programming languages"* or *"develop software"*. These are more
informative than trivially distant skills like *"negotiate contracts"*,
because the model must learn fine-grained distinctions within the same
domain rather than merely separating unrelated concepts. During
training, correct sentence–skill pairings act as positives while all
other skills in the same batch act as negatives --- with the hardest
cases (same-domain, wrong skill) driving most of the learning signal.
This gives the model a scalable way to learn ranking behaviour across
the full ~13,000-skill taxonomy without a separate classifier for each
skill.

```{=html}
<svg viewBox="0 0 620 370" width="620" style="font-family: system-ui, -apple-system, sans-serif; max-width: 100%; display: block; margin: 1.2rem auto;">
  <!-- Easy negatives zone -->
```

This approach is well suited to online job ads because employers often
describe the same skill in many different ways. By learning semantic
proximity rather than relying on exact wording, the model can recover
skills even when the phrasing differs from the ESCO label itself.

Our approach also avoids relying only on one averaged sentence
representation. Instead, the encoder can attend more strongly to the
parts of a sentence that are most diagnostic for a given skill, which
is particularly useful when a single sentence mentions several tasks,
tools, or competencies at once. This token-level attention mechanism
has been shown to improve matching quality in multi-skill sentences
(<a class="paper-link" href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.09119" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer">Sun, 2026<span class="source-link-ext">↗</span></a>;
<a class="paper-link" href="https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/11074185" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer">Decorte et al., 2025<span class="source-link-ext">↗</span></a>).

**Similarity threshold calibration.** &ensp; Not every high-ranking
candidate is a true match. Following established practice in ESCO
skill extraction
(<a class="paper-link" href="https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/11074185" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer">Decorte et al., 2025<span class="source-link-ext">↗</span></a>;
<a class="paper-link" href="https://recsyshr.aau.dk/wp-content/uploads/2025/09/RecSysHR2025-paper_5.pdf" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer">Bielinski &amp; Brazier, 2025<span class="source-link-ext">↗</span></a>),
we retain only those candidates whose cosine similarity exceeds a
calibrated threshold. The threshold is tuned on held-out benchmark
data (the same HOUSE and TECH datasets used to evaluate overall
pipeline performance) by selecting the value that maximises the
trade-off between precision and recall. This step filters out
low-confidence matches and controls the total number of skills
assigned per posting.

```{mermaid}
%%| fig-cap: "Skill-to-ESCO matching pipeline"
%%{init: {'flowchart': {'htmlLabels': true, 'nodeSpacing': 50, 'rankSpacing': 55}, 'themeVariables': {'fontSize': '13px'}} }%%
flowchart TD
    A["Skill-relevant sentences"] -->|"encode"| B["Contrastive bi-encoder"]
    B -->|"768-d vector"| C["Sentence embedding"]

    D[("ESCO skill catalogue<br/>~13 000 entries")] -->|"pre-computed<br/>768-d vectors"| E["Reference embedding matrix"]

    C --> F{"Cosine similarity ranking"}
    E --> F

    F -->|"top-k candidates"| G["Candidate ESCO skills<br/>with similarity scores"]
    G -->|"score ≥ calibrated threshold"| I["Final matched ESCO skills"]
```
::::

:::: {#pipeline-step-05 .step-detail}
#### [Step 05]{.step-badge .step-badge-indigo} Job title standardisation

Raw job titles are highly variable: the same role may appear as
"Inżynier oprogramowania", "Backend Developer", "Programista",
"Full-Stack Developer", or "Senior Software Engineer". Likewise,
an analytical role may appear as "Analityk danych", "BI Analyst",
"Specjalista ds. raportowania", or "Data Analyst". Because postings
have been harmonised into Polish in the translation step, the
standardisation step works on a common-language title field.
Mapping each title to a standardised ESCO occupation enables comparable
occupational analysis and serves as the bridge to sector classification
in the next step.

Titles are first cleaned by removing common noise (embedded locations,
salary ranges, seniority prefixes). The cleaned titles are then
embedded using
<a class="paper-link" href="https://huggingface.co/TechWolf/JobBERT-v3" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer">JobBERT-v3<span class="source-link-ext">↗</span></a>,
a domain-specific open model pre-trained on large-scale job market
data. We pre-compute embeddings for all ~3,000 ESCO occupation labels
and store them in a <a class="paper-link" href="https://github.com/facebookresearch/faiss" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer">FAISS<span class="source-link-ext">↗</span></a>
vector index for fast retrieval. Each job title is matched to the
nearest ESCO occupation by cosine similarity, with the similarity
score retained for downstream quality filtering.

```{mermaid}
%%| fig-cap: "Job title standardisation"
%%{init: {'flowchart': {'htmlLabels': true, 'nodeSpacing': 50, 'rankSpacing': 55}, 'themeVariables': {'fontSize': '13px'}} }%%
flowchart TD
    A["Translated job title"] --> B["Title cleaning<br/><i style='font-size:0.8em;color:#64748b'>(remove locations, salaries, prefixes)</i>"]
    B -->|"cleaned text"| C["JobBERT-v3 encoder"]
    C -->|"768-d vector"| D["Title embedding"]

    D -->|"query"| F{"FAISS nearest-neighbour search"}

    E[("ESCO occupation index<br/>~3 000 occupations<br/><i style='font-size:0.8em;color:#64748b'>pre-computed 768-d vectors</i>")] -->|"index"| F

    F -->|"best match + cosine score"| G["Standardised ESCO occupation"]
```
::::

:::: {#pipeline-step-06 .step-detail}
#### [Step 06]{.step-badge .step-badge-green} Sector classification (ISIC/NACE)

Assigning an economic sector to each job posting enables analysis of
skill demand by industry---a dimension that is critical for targeted
workforce development and industrial policy. We classify postings into
the **ISIC/NACE** industry taxonomy. The underlying crosswalk uses the
full NACE Rev. 2.1 classification maintained by Eurostat, which provides
finer sub-division detail (3- and 4-digit codes) than ISIC. However,
because this report analyses sectoral demand at the **2-digit division
level**, the results are identical under both systems: at 2 digits,
NACE Rev. 2.1 and ISIC Rev. 5 share the same division codes and
boundaries
(<a class="paper-link" href="https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/documents/3859598/21633320/KS-GQ-24-007-EN-N.pdf" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer">Eurostat, 2024<span class="source-link-ext">↗</span></a>).
All results in this report are therefore directly comparable with any
analysis using either framework.

The assignment relies on the official
<a class="paper-link" href="https://esco.ec.europa.eu/en/about-esco/escopedia/escopedia/nace" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer">ESCO-to-NACE crosswalk<span class="source-link-ext">↗</span></a>,
which links each ESCO occupation to one or more ISIC/NACE activity
codes. Three resolution tiers handle different levels of ambiguity:

1. **One-to-one mapping** --- the ESCO occupation maps to a single
   ISIC/NACE code. The assignment is deterministic.
2. **Same 2-digit code** --- all candidate codes share the same 2-digit
   division (e.g. all fall under *C26*). The shared division is assigned
   directly, since finer sub-division differences are below the
   reporting threshold.
3. **Ambiguous multi-division cases** --- candidates span different
   ISIC/NACE divisions. We resolve these by embedding the job title and
   description together with each candidate activity label using a
   multilingual sentence-transformer
   (<a class="paper-link" href="https://huggingface.co/sentence-transformers/paraphrase-multilingual-MiniLM-L12-v2" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer">paraphrase-multilingual-MiniLM-L12-v2<span class="source-link-ext">↗</span></a>)
   and selecting the candidate with the highest cosine similarity. A
   confidence margin between the top two candidates is recorded to
   support post-hoc quality auditing.

```{mermaid}
%%| fig-cap: "ISIC/NACE sector classification"
%%{init: {'flowchart': {'htmlLabels': true, 'nodeSpacing': 30, 'rankSpacing': 45, 'curve': 'basis'}, 'themeVariables': {'fontSize': '13px'}} }%%
flowchart LR
    A["ESCO occupation<br/><i style='font-size:0.8em;color:#64748b'>from Step 05</i>"]
      -->|"look up"| B[("ESCO → ISIC/NACE crosswalk<br/><i style='font-size:0.8em;color:#64748b'>official mapping table</i>")]
    B --> C{"Number of candidate<br/>ISIC/NACE codes?"}

    C -->|"exactly 1"| D["Deterministic<br/>assignment"]
    C -->|"≥ 2, same 2-digit code"| E["Assign shared<br/>ISIC/NACE division"]
    C -->|"≥ 2, different divisions"| F["Embedding-based disambiguation<br/><i style='font-size:0.8em;color:#64748b'>encode job text + each candidate ISIC/NACE label</i>"]

    F -->|"384-d vectors"| H{"Cosine similarity<br/>comparison"}
    H -->|"highest score"| I["Assigned ISIC/NACE code<br/>+ confidence margin"]

    D --> J["Final sector label"]
    E --> J
    I --> J

    classDef step fill:#eef4fb,stroke:#1d4e89,stroke-width:1px,color:#15314B;
    classDef data fill:#fef3c7,stroke:#b45309,stroke-width:1px,color:#7c2d12;
    classDef out  fill:#dcfce7,stroke:#166534,stroke-width:1px,color:#14532d;
    class A,D,E,F,I step;
    class B data;
    class C,H step;
    class J out;
```
::::

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
Our pipeline outperforms the current state of the art by approximately
3 percentage points in RP@5 on the HOUSE and TECH benchmark datasets
reported by <span class="paper-ref" data-tooltip="Decorte, J. J., Van Hautte, J., Develder, C., and Demeester, T. 2025. Efficient Text Encoders for Labor Market Analysis. IEEE Access."><a class="paper-link" href="https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/abstract/document/11079977/" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer">Decorte et al. (2025)</a></span>.
These benchmarks consist of job postings annotated with ESCO
gold-standard skill labels by human experts, against which model
predictions are evaluated. The reported RP@5 scores are 0.822 and 0.838,
respectively.
:::
:::

::: {.section-card}
### AI Skills Demand

The demand for AI-related skills is highly dynamic, with new
technologies and tools emerging rapidly while others become obsolete.
This makes it difficult to track AI skill demand using static
taxonomies alone.

Lightcast captures highly granular and technology-specific signals, such
as individual AI tools, models, copilots, libraries, and chatbot
platforms. This makes it well suited to detecting early changes in
employer demand. We start from the benchmark list of 350 AI skills
identified by
<span class="paper-ref" data-tooltip="Martins-Neto, A., Liu, Y., Khurana, S., and Porras Lopez, J. M. 2026. Click, Code, Earn: The Returns to Digital Skills. World Bank."><a class="paper-link" href="https://documents1.worldbank.org/curated/en/099451102172652767/pdf/IDU-e779b9af-e9b1-43ae-a2c5-9679dbf2d829.pdf" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer">Martins-Neto et al. (2026)</a></span>
and extend it with 114 additional skills that have since appeared in the
Lightcast taxonomy, bringing the current total to 464 AI skills.

To make the full list policy-readable, we organize these 464 skills into
four primary categories and eight cross-cutting tags. The primary
categories are mutually exclusive and capture the fundamental domain of
each skill. The tags are non-exclusive and highlight secondary
dimensions that cut across categories.

```{=html}
<div class="ai-category-grid" id="ai-category-cards"></div>
<div id="ai-tag-chart"></div>
<p class="notes source-note">Source: Lightcast AI skills taxonomy; Martins-Neto et al. (2026); authors' categorization.</p>
```
:::

### Green Skills Demand

::: {.section-card}
#### Identification approach

Green skills are identified by matching the ESCO skills extracted from
job postings (Step 04 of the pipeline) against the official
<a class="paper-link" href="https://esco.ec.europa.eu/en/about-esco/publications/publication/green-skills-and-knowledge-concepts-labelling-esco" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer">ESCO Green Skills and Knowledge Collection<span class="source-link-ext">↗</span></a>,
a curated subset of roughly 830 skills and knowledge concepts that the
European Commission classifies as relevant to the green transition.

A job posting is counted as "green" if at least one of its matched ESCO
skills belongs to this collection. Because the ESCO green taxonomy is
broad and includes some entries that are only tangentially related to
environmental sustainability, we apply a manual review step: each
matched skill is classified as either **genuine green** or **false
positive** based on whether its presence in a job posting plausibly
signals demand for environmental or sustainability competences.

```{=html}
<div class="kpi-grid" id="green-kpi-cards"></div>
```
:::

::: {.section-card}

#### False positives

Not all skills in the ESCO green collection carry a clear environmental
signal when they appear in Polish job postings. Skills such as *building
codes*, *vehicle type-approval*, or *warehouse management software* are
part of the ESCO green taxonomy but frequently appear in postings where
the role has no meaningful green dimension. After matching, we manually
flag these as false positives and exclude them from the headline green
skill counts. The full list of excluded skills is shown below.

```{=html}
<details class="green-fp-details">
  <summary>Show excluded false-positive skills (click to expand)</summary>
  <div class="data-table-wrap" id="green-false-positives-list"></div>
</details>
```
:::

::::: {.section-card .map-shell}
#### Regional green skill demand

The map shows the share of job postings with at least one genuine green
skill in each voivodeship. Regional variation is moderate: shares range
from roughly 2.5% to 4.0%, with higher concentrations in voivodeships
where construction, energy, and agricultural sectors are more prominent.

The chart ranks the 15 KZIS (Polish Classification of Occupations)

### Jobs for Ukrainians

::: {.section-card}
#### Background

Polish job postings on Pracuj.pl can carry an explicit
**Запрошуємо працівників з України / Jobs for Ukrainians** badge, added by
the employer to signal that the role is open to (and the workplace is
prepared to support) Ukrainian candidates. The tag was introduced
shortly after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022
as part of Pracuj.pl's response to the wave of refugees arriving in
Poland — see
<a class="paper-link" href="https://media.pracuj.pl/179412-grupa-pracuj-dla-ukrainy" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer">Grupa Pracuj dla Ukrainy<span class="source-link-ext">↗</span></a>.

We retrieve the badge by parsing the `data-test="sections-benefit-ukrainian-friendly"`
HTML element on each posting's detail page, and join the result back to
the structured fields in `job_ads`. Looking at where this tag appears
tells us which **regions, industries and occupations** are most actively
opening up to workers from Ukraine — and by extension, to foreign labour
more broadly. It also reveals where employer demand and refugee supply
overlap most strongly.

```{=html}
<div class="kpi-grid" id="ukr-kpi-cards"></div>
```
:::

::::: {.section-card .map-shell}
#### Regional intensity

The map shows the share of all 2025 Pracuj.pl postings in each
voivodeship that carry the Jobs-for-Ukrainians tag. Małopolskie leads
clearly (around 14% of postings), followed by Lubuskie, Łódzkie,
Lubelskie and Dolnośląskie — a mix of regions with large refugee
populations (Małopolskie, Dolnośląskie), border-area logistics hubs and
food-processing clusters (Lubuskie, Lubelskie, Łódzkie). Mazowieckie has
the largest absolute number of tagged offers but a lower share, since
its labour market is dominated by professional and IT roles where the
tag is less commonly used.

```{=html}
<div class="figure-caption-title"><strong>Figure 34a.</strong> Share of postings tagged 'Jobs for Ukrainians', by voivodeship (2025)</div>
<div id="ukr-regional-map"></div>
<div class="map-caption source-note">Source: Pracuj.pl postings with <code>data-test="sections-benefit-ukrainian-friendly"</code>; authors' parsing.</div>
```
:::::

::: {.section-card}
#### Demand intensity vs Ukrainian-friendly share

A natural question is whether voivodeships with a **hotter labour
market** — measured as total job offers per 100k labour force — are also
the ones where employers more often choose to **flag a posting as
Ukrainian-friendly**. Plotting the within-region share (Y, %) against
total offer intensity (X) gives a much weaker relationship than one
might expect: across the 16 voivodeships, **Pearson r ≈ +0.24**,
**Spearman ρ ≈ +0.26**, **R² ≈ 0.06**. In other words, demand intensity
explains very little of the cross-regional variation in how often the
badge is used.

The clearest outlier is **Małopolskie**, sitting well above the cloud at
≈14% of postings tagged despite only mid-range overall intensity — a
likely echo of Kraków's large post-2022 Ukrainian diaspora.
**Kujawsko-Pomorskie** (~6.6%) and **Podkarpackie** (~7.0%) sit clearly
below the cloud, while **Mazowieckie** — by far the densest labour
market — is exactly average on the share dimension (~9.7%). This
suggests the Ukrainian-friendly tag tracks **demographic factors**
(refugee settlement patterns) and **sectoral mix** much more than
overall hiring intensity.

```{=html}
<div class="figure-caption-title"><strong>Figure 34b.</strong> Total offers per 100k labour force vs share of offers tagged 'Jobs for Ukrainians', by voivodeship</div>
<div id="ukr-density-scatter"></div>
<p class="notes source-note">Source: Pracuj.pl postings; Statistics Poland (BAEL) labour-force averages 2025; authors' computation. Each marker is one of the 16 voivodeships; the dashed line is the OLS fit.</p>
```
:::

::::: {.section-card .map-shell}
#### Powiat-level demand intensity

Switching the denominator from labour force (only published by GUS at
the voivodeship level) to **employed-by-residence** (the closest
powiat-level proxy, available monthly via the GUS BDL P4280 series)
brings the offer-intensity picture down to all **380 powiats**. The
density gradient is dominated by a handful of metropolitan magnets —
Warszawa, Kraków, Wrocław, Poznań, Trójmiasto, Łódź — together with
the suburban "donut" powiats around them (e.g. *poznański*, *pruszkowski*,
*piaseczyński*, *wrocławski*) where offer-to-employed ratios run an
order of magnitude above the rural average. Most of central-eastern
Poland and the Bieszczady–Roztocze belt sit below 1,000 offers /
100k employed.

```{=html}
<div class="figure-caption-title"><strong>Figure 34c.</strong> Total job offers per 100k employed (residence-based), by powiat (2025)</div>
<div id="ukr-powiat-intensity-map" style="height:640px;"></div>
<div class="map-caption source-note">Source: Pracuj.pl postings (2025); GUS BDL P4280 — employed persons in the national economy by place of residence (January 2025). Colour scale capped at the 95th percentile to preserve resolution outside the metropolitan magnets.</div>
```
:::::

::::: {.section-card .map-shell}
#### Powiat-level Ukrainian-friendly share

Zooming in from the 16 voivodeships to all 380 powiats preserves
the overall national share (~9.7%) but reveals strong sub-regional
variation that the voivodeship view averages out. The badge is
heavily concentrated in **western and central rural-industrial
powiats** — Lower Silesian copper-belt counties (e.g. *polkowicki* at
≈30%), the Lubelskie countryside east of the Vistula, the Mazovian
food-processing belt around *kozienicki* and *lipski*, and frontier
counties along the German border (e.g. *słubicki*, *świebodziński*).
At the other extreme, several large **city-on-county-rights** labour
markets (Toruń, Krosno, Kalisz) and small mono-industrial powiats
(*obornicki*, *ostrowiecki*) sit below 6%.

```{=html}
<div class="figure-caption-title"><strong>Figure 34d.</strong> Share of postings tagged 'Jobs for Ukrainians', by powiat (2025)</div>
<div id="ukr-powiat-map" style="height:640px;"></div>
<div class="map-caption source-note">Source: Pracuj.pl postings with <code>data-test="sections-benefit-ukrainian-friendly"</code>; powiat resolved via TERYT SIMC + GUGiK UUG geocoding (see methods). Colour scale capped at 25%.</div>
```
:::::

::: {.section-card}
#### Demand intensity vs UA-friendly share — powiat level

Crossing the two powiat layers — **offers per 100k employed** on the
X-axis and within-powiat Ukrainian-friendly share on the Y-axis —
confirms what the voivodeship plot already hinted at: there is
**essentially no relationship** between how dense a local labour
market is and how often employers there flag jobs for Ukrainian
workers. Restricted to the 294 powiats with at least 200 postings,
**Pearson r ≈ −0.16**, **Spearman ρ ≈ −0.11**, **R² ≈ 0.024** — i.e.
demand intensity explains roughly 2% of the cross-powiat variation in
the badge's use.

The major metropolitan magnets (Warszawa, Kraków, Wrocław, Poznań,
Gdańsk) cluster around the national average (~9–11%) despite very
different intensity levels, while the high-share powiats sit at
**low-to-medium** intensity. The takeaway mirrors the regional
analysis: the Ukrainian-friendly badge tracks **sectoral mix and
refugee settlement geography** much more than overall hiring
intensity.

```{=html}
<div class="figure-caption-title"><strong>Figure 34e.</strong> Job offers per 100k employed vs share of offers tagged 'Jobs for Ukrainians', by powiat</div>
<div id="ukr-powiat-scatter"></div>
<p class="notes source-note">Source: Pracuj.pl postings (2025); GUS BDL P4280 employed-by-residence (January 2025). Bubble size ∝ √(total offers); only powiats with ≥200 postings included in the OLS fit.</p>
```
:::

::: {.section-card}
#### Industries (NACE sections)

Aggregated to the top-level NACE section, the Ukrainian-friendly tag is
strongly concentrated in service sectors that absorb low-barrier labour:
**accommodation and food service (I)** stands out at roughly a third of
all postings, followed by **transportation and storage (H)** and
**manufacturing (C)**. Sections dominated by professional services and
public administration use the tag much less frequently.

```{=html}
<div class="figure-caption-title"><strong>Figure 34f.</strong> NACE sections with the highest share of Ukrainian-friendly postings</div>
<div id="ukr-industries-section-chart"></div>
<p class="notes source-note">Source: Pracuj.pl + ESCO→NACE crosswalk. Sections shown have at least 5,000 postings.</p>
```
:::

::: {.section-card}
#### Industries (NACE divisions)

Drilling down to NACE divisions exposes the specific niches driving
demand for Ukrainian workers. By share, the leaders are food retail and
restaurants (G47.5, G47.22, I56.11, G47.11), passenger road transport
(H49.32, H49.33) and goods road transport (H49.41) — sectors with high
turnover, language-tolerant tasks and a strong refugee employment
footprint. By absolute volume, **restaurants (I56.11)**, **warehousing
(H52.1)** and **programming activities (K62.1)** dominate, the last
reflecting the large pool of Ukrainian IT specialists who relocated
after 2022.

```{=html}
<div class="figure-caption-title"><strong>Figure 34g.</strong> NACE divisions with the highest share of Ukrainian-friendly postings</div>
<div id="ukr-industries-share-chart"></div>
<div class="figure-caption-title" style="margin-top:1rem;"><strong>Figure 34h.</strong> NACE divisions with the largest absolute number of Ukrainian-friendly postings</div>
<div id="ukr-industries-count-chart"></div>
<p class="notes source-note">Source: Pracuj.pl + ESCO→NACE crosswalk. Only divisions with at least 500 postings are ranked.</p>
```
:::

::: {.section-card}
#### Occupational categories

Using Pracuj.pl's own narrow job categories (`job_category_narrow`), the
tag is most prevalent in food-related and manual-labour roles —
*Food products*, *Hospitality staff*, *Manual labour*,
*Couriers / delivery* — and in hospitality and personal-services
categories such as *Hotel operations* and *Hairdresser / beautician*. The
absolute-volume ranking confirms that gastronomy, courier and warehouse
categories together account for the bulk of Ukrainian-friendly hiring.

```{=html}
<div class="figure-caption-title"><strong>Figure 34i.</strong> Narrow job categories with the highest share of Ukrainian-friendly postings</div>
<div id="ukr-categories-narrow-share-chart"></div>
<div class="figure-caption-title" style="margin-top:1rem;"><strong>Figure 34j.</strong> Narrow job categories with the largest absolute number of Ukrainian-friendly postings</div>
<div id="ukr-categories-narrow-count-chart"></div>
<p class="notes source-note">Source: Pracuj.pl <code>job_category_narrow</code>. Only categories with at least 500 postings are ranked.</p>
```
:::

{{< include includes/wb_ukr_nace.qmd >}}

::: {.section-card}
#### Seniority and contract types

The tag overwhelmingly attaches to **manual-worker**
roles — over a fifth of such postings are Ukrainian-friendly — and to a
hybrid `manager / supervisor` shift-leader category common in retail and
gastronomy. Specialist, expert and director roles see the tag much
less. On the contract side, **temporary employment contracts** and **contracts of mandate** carry the
tag most often, reflecting the prevalence of short-tenure agency-style
hiring in the segments where Ukrainian workers are most actively
recruited; standard permanent contracts and B2B contracts use the tag
considerably less.
